verdicts.direction_check:
The direction is sound: a home is walls that leak, plus supplies that differ between buildings and run down. It matches ROADMAP core 4 ('ผนังกั้น'), core 6 ('ปิดแน่นไหม') and lines 343/385/390. I would change six things.

1. Put the cheap 'walls count' fixes before any new item: spot_safe counting only outer openings, sleep and wake checks that respect walls and floors (the lens missed these, M1), and muffling by a sealed building. They cost S, need no art, and are the most direct fix for what the user calls ขัดๆ at home.

2. Respect three agreed designs the lens ran over. Rain filling the rooftop tank was agreed in core 6, so tune TANK_RAIN down rather than remove it. 'ลากเฟอร์นิเจอร์' is planned in phase 2, so present bracing as its first step rather than ruling dragging out. Line 341 says others can walk into a claimed home, so padlocks that keep people out conflict with it.

3. The appraisal line must hold only what the player has seen. An omniscient readout at the door breaks realism and the tension of scouting.

4. Several findings are symptoms of the 4-minute day: a shower lasting 9-20 game hours, rice cooked in 7 s, a 65-s night. Deciding the clock first is right, but prefer a longer day over real-minute timers.

5. The lens underweights visible interior realism that costs little. Every fridge is drawn as a glass shop cooler, and flat units are identical wards. The 1-m interior walls are already being mocked by another lens. It also promotes flats as homes without noticing that they can't cook (M2) or be held (M3).

6. It proposes too many new systems for a solo beginner (lamps, heat, dengue, spirit house, charcoal, padlocks, pushing the bike, condo doors). Trim each round to one or two new Things after the data tuning. A small extra: your claimed home isn't marked on the map (city_map.gd pins are manual only). Among identical shophouses that makes 'go home' harder than it should be; auto-pinning the claimed bed's building is an S fix.

review.summary: Fresh-eyes verdict: the Thai details are right. Scooters with delivery boxes are parked nose-in at shop fronts, and inside there is a spirit house, a red altar and safe, a water jar (โอ่ง) with its dipper, a meshed food safe (ตู้กับข้าว), a gas stove with a red LPG cylinder and a standing fan. The trouble is that people and bikes are life-size and drawn in 3/4, while cars, vans, pickups, songthaews, tuk-tuks and army trucks are shrunk to about 55-70% of real size, and the ones parked north-south are flat top-down stickers. So they don't read as steel boxes you could hide behind, climb or get into, and the tuk-tuk and songthaew can't be recognised. Homes have the right furniture, but every shophouse has the same set in the same places. None of them shows who lived there. The toilets sit in the open, the home fridge is a shop drinks cooler, the flats have no doors, and walls read as dark trenches. Recommended direction: (1) one scale rule: anything a body touches is life-size; only distances are squeezed. (2) One projection rule: every solid object shows its top plus its south face, like the buildings, through one data-driven 'box vehicle' drawer that also serves wrecks, traffic jams and later driving. (3) Homes get a 'who lived here and how they left' layer baked into the floor chunk, rather than more furniture types. (4) Tie vehicles into the core loop and the home: storage on the bike, the bike sleeps inside the shop behind the shutter, and jammed evacuation roads with trunks to search. Do first: fix the rider's posture (S), then the box drawer with true sizes, in one GEN bump together with the jams and the parking-direction rule. For homes, the household-story layer plus the fridge, bathroom and flat-door fixes. New vehicles in this order: bicycle (silent, no fuel), then tuk-tuk, then cars with the driver hidden inside (no new character views). Skip the skateboard.
strengths: Night riding sells the mood: the headlight cone on Phahon Yothin with the tail light glowing on the orange box (v05) is instantly atmospheric. Keep the headlight and the dark street around it.

Parked bikes behave like real Bangkok bikes: nose-in in front of shophouses with the tail light and mirror stalks showing (art_01 y~370-480, h01, 18 bottom), and on pavements across the kerb (v13 ~690,520; v20; 02_phahon_bts). Keep these parking rules.
The delivery box on the rider (v01, v03, v05) and on parked bikes (v13 top-left, green box in 02 ~330,140) reads as 2020s Bangkok at a glance. Keep it and make it useful (see V6).

Vehicles drawn side-on read immediately. The bus with its windows, doors, wheels and route sign (v17), the kerb-parked sedans (12_ratchawithi bottom, v01 top) and the army truck at the sandbag and barrier checkpoint (v18) are the best vehicle art in the game. Use them as the colour and detail reference for the new drawer.
The outbreak story is in the wrecks: a van under a fallen lamppost, a burnt car, blood drag marks (v12, 12_ratchawithi, v16 left).

The Thai household objects are specific and correct: spirit house on a post (h01), red Chinese altar, safe and gold display cases (h02), the jar (โอ่ง) with a pink dipper on top, the squat toilet, the meshed food safe, the gas stove with a red LPG cylinder (h03), the standing fan and wooden upstairs floor (h05), and bare hanging bulbs.
The shophouse layout is right: shop front, middle room, back kitchen with a back door, stairs, bedrooms upstairs, hatch to the roof (h04, h05). Keep this layout and vary what goes in it.
Sleeping at night in a warm lamp-lit room while the soi outside is blue-dark (h06) is a strong 'home' moment.
Thai shop signs with jokes (ร้านตัดผม หนีไปวัด) and made-up names fit the realism-with-humour tone.
The scooter-to-rider proportion is right (the scooter is about 2 cells, about 1.9 m), and all 4 riding views read as a person on a bike (v01-v03).

findings.title: North-south parked cars, vans, pickups and songthaews read as flat stickers, not solid vehicles
findings.observation: FACT: vehicles parked facing north or south are drawn almost straight from above: a coloured rectangle with one or two dark window bands, a light strip and two wheel stubs at the south end, and no visible height (v11 blue car, v12 taxi and blue car, v14_van, v15_pickup, v16_songthaew, red car at the bottom of v18). Vehicles facing east or west are side views with wheels, windows and doors (v01 top, v17 bus and sedan, v18 army truck, bottom kerb of 12_ratchawithi). Wrecks at an angle rotate the same art. In 12_ratchawithi top-right, the overturned car is a rotated, upside-down side view. In 02_phahon_bts bottom-right, a side-view sedan tilted about 15 degrees on the pavement looks like it is driving up a ramp.
findings.evidence: v11 (car 588-680 x 148-332 px at z4; the player's head covers its middle), v14_van (583-673 x 178-355), v15_pickup, v16_songthaew (578-667 x 165-340); compare v17 (bus 350-940 x 85-275, reads instantly) and 12_ratchawithi (parked side-view cars at the bottom kerb read well; the overturned car top-right and the white van top-middle look odd); 02_phahon_bts bottom-right tilted sedan.
findings.why: OPINION: the world is drawn in 3/4. Buildings show a roof plus a south facade and characters stand upright, so a vehicle with no south face has no height. The eye reads it as a mat on the road, and a player standing just south of it looks like he is standing on it. That is exactly the 'can I get into it?' test failing. Two drawing styles also make the same car look like two different objects depending on which way it is parked. This is the main reason vehicles feel off, even though the bus (side view) looks great.
findings.suggestion: Build one generic 'box vehicle' drawer. Each type is 2-4 boxes (chassis, cabin, cargo box or canopy) described by rows in a data table: length, width, height, z, colour, window pattern, light and plate positions. Draw the visible faces by projecting the box corners with the game's 3/4 squash: the top faces foreshortened, plus the faces that point south (the rear or front face for north-south, the side for east-west, two faces for diagonals), wheels peeking under the south face, and a soft shadow. Use the same code for wrecks at any angle (tipped over = a different face up) and later for cars you can drive. Bake each parked prop into a texture once. Take colours and details from the current side views (v17 bus, 12 sedans).
findings.scope_check: No character views involved. The art stays in code, but it is one drawer plus data rows instead of hand-drawn art per type and direction. Parked props are static and baked once, so there is no per-frame cost. On its own it doesn't change city generation (same props, same cells); combine it with V2's sizes in one GEN bump.

findings.title: Vehicles are toy-sized next to people and next to bikes; only the bikes are life-size
findings.observation: FACT, measured on the screenshots (pixels / zoom / 16 = cells, 1 cell = about 1 m): scooter about 106 px at z3 = 2.2 cells (v20; real about 1.9 m, correct). Sedan 92x184 px at z4 = 1.4 x 2.9 cells (v11; real 1.8 x 4.5 m). Van (v14_van, about 90x178) and pickup (v15_pickup, about 90x170) are the same box as the sedan (real 5.3 m and 5.1 m). Bus 590 px = 9.2 cells (v17; real 12 m). The army truck's canvas top is about 80 px above the ground line while the player is about 120 px tall (v18; a real truck is about 3 m, 1.8 times a person). So a car is only 1.3 times a scooter's length (real 2.4 times) and the army truck is shorter than the survivor. Road lanes, on the other hand, are real scale: in v01 there are about 3 cells from the kerb to the centre dashes. The brief mentions a single global VEHICLE_SCALE of 1.6.
findings.evidence: v11, v14_van, v15_pickup, v16_songthaew (the player's head reaches the middle of the vehicle), v18 (c_v18_army crop: the truck roof is at the player's eye level), v20 (scooter), v17 (bus), v01 (lane width).
findings.why: Realism: a van the size of a sedan and an army truck shorter than a man break the 'real Bangkok' read at first glance. Gameplay: a car should be a big steel box that blocks half a soi, that you can hide behind or climb onto for safety, and whose size says 'safe but clumsy compared to a bike'. At 60% size it says 'prop'. OPINION on the root cause: the 2.5x squeeze of the district was also applied to vehicles. Squeeze distances, never the things a body touches (vehicles, furniture, doors).
findings.suggestion: Replace the global VEHICLE_SCALE with true per-type sizes in cells (length x width x height; a character reads as about 1.7 m): sedan and taxi 4.3 x 1.8 x 1.5, pickup 5.1 x 1.9 x 1.8, van 5.3 x 1.9 x 2.2, songthaew 5.1 x 1.9 x 2.3, tuk-tuk 3.0 x 1.4 x 1.8, bus 11 x 2.5 x 3.2, army truck 7 x 2.4 x 3.0. Keep them in the same data table as V1. In 3-cell sois, allow at most one car, parked tight to a wall. Real Bangkok sois are like that: the car takes half the soi and bikes squeeze past. Recheck CLIMB: a bus or truck roof should need a boost or a crate, which makes it a real vantage point.
findings.scope_check: Data plus drawing constants, no new views. Bigger collision footprints change placement, so it needs a CityGen.GEN bump; do it in the same bump as V1, V4 (parking direction) and V5 (jams). Static props, so no per-frame cost.

findings.title: The rider sits like a chopper or sport rider on a 110 cc scooter
findings.observation: FACT: side view (v01, crop c_v01_rider): the torso is hunched forward, the face is almost over the grips and the fists are pulled in to the chest. Back view (v03, c_v03_rider): the hands are at jaw or ear height beside the head, the elbows are winged out and the knees are splayed wider than the bike. Front view (v02) reads fine, but there are no mirror stalks above the bar, while parked bikes do show them (art_01, about y 370).
findings.why: Every Thai player knows how a scooter is ridden: upright or slightly slouched, arms relaxed forward and down, hands at stomach height, knees inside the legshield, feet flat on the floorboard. On an underbone like the Wave or Cub, the knees hug the frame. The current pose reads as 'not from here', and it is on screen every second of riding. It is the cheapest high-visibility fix in this list.
findings.suggestion: Make the rig anchors per bike class, as data next to BIKE_MODELS: seat, grips, feet, knee spread, torso lean, head pitch. Scooters (click, pcx, nmax, scoopy, filano, ev, forza, vespa): grips at about elbow height and close in, knees together, feet forward on the floor. Step-through and underbone (wave, cub): grips a little lower, knees around the frame. Sport: lean forward, grips low and forward. Trail and adventure (trail, adv): upright, wide grips, feet on pegs, knees out. Classic (enfield): upright. The head looks down the road, not at the bars. Draw the mirror stalks while riding too. Later, as rig poses: show the half-helmet item (ROADMAP line 157) when worn, and a side-saddle pillion (very Thai).
findings.scope_check: Anchor and pose data in the existing 4 views, so clothes follow automatically. No new art beyond the mirror stalks. No extra per-frame cost.

findings.title: The Thai vehicles can't be recognised by silhouette, and parked cars face against left-hand traffic
findings.observation: FACT: the tuk-tuk (v13 about 580,220; crop c_v13_tuk) is a black flat canopy with a yellow fringe, two equal wheels and a red box, so it reads as a noodle or food cart. The same object on the right of v05 (about 1035,410) can't be told apart from a vendor cart. The songthaew (v16) and the red pickup (v15_pickup) are both red rectangles with one dark band. The van (v14_van, v15_van) is a white box the size of a sedan. The bus route sign is an empty orange box (v17 about 875,73). Every north-south vehicle shows its headlights at the south end, whichever side of the road it is on: the v12 taxi and blue car, v14_van, v15_pickup and v16 at the west kerb, and the v18 red vehicle in the west half of a two-way road. Thailand drives on the left, so those face against traffic.
findings.evidence: v13, v05, v15_pickup vs v16_songthaew, v14_van, v17 sign, v12/v14/v15/v16/v18 (white lights at the south end while at the west kerb). ROADMAP line 311 (the old van terminal at Victory Monument is in this zone) and line 314 (Thai city vehicles).
findings.why: For Thai players these vehicles ARE the 'this is Bangkok' moments: the tuk-tuk, the songthaew, the two-tone taxi, the Victory Monument van. If they don't read, the district feels generic. Parked cars facing the wrong way feel subtly foreign to anyone who drives here.
findings.suggestion: Silhouette must-haves per type, as rows in the V1 table. Tuk-tuk: 1 front wheel and 2 rear, a narrow cab nose with a handlebar, a curved canopy with coloured trim, open sides with a bench. Songthaew: pickup cab plus a tall roofed rear with two side benches and a step and grab rail at the back. Pickup: cab plus an open bed with side walls and things in it (water jugs, LPG cylinders, a steel cage rack). Van: high roof, roof rack, sliding-door line, a route card in the windscreen. Taxi: two-tone with a roof sign in generic words. Plates: white with black text for private cars, yellow for taxis and public or commercial vehicles (the real Thai convention; no brands). Paint route numbers in the bus sign. Parking rule: at a kerb, face with left-hand traffic; wrecks stay random.
findings.scope_check: Data rows for the V1 drawer (do it after V1). The parking-direction rule is a placement change, so a GEN bump: batch it with V2 and V5. No views, no per-frame cost.

findings.title: Every home is the same furnished set; nothing shows who lived there until last week
findings.observation: FACT: the back kitchen is identical, object for object and in the same places, in the gold shop (h03), the minimart (17) and the shop in 09: sink, stove with a red gas bottle, glass drinks cooler, meshed food safe, jar with dipper, squat toilet, stairs. Upstairs is identical in the gold shop (h05, h07) and the minimart (19): back room with bed, fan, drawers and a small table; an empty middle room with only the hatch; a front room with a bed and a gold-trimmed cabinet. Floors are spotless. In any of these screenshots I see no shoes at the door, clothes, laundry, calendar, family photo, school bag, TV, eating table, plastic stools, toys, medicine, or signs of panic (open drawers, a half-packed suitcase, a knocked-over chair). In the bedroom at night (h06, crop c_h06_bed), the sleeper's black shoe soles stick out under the blanket.
findings.evidence: h03 vs 17 vs 09 (the same back half); h05 vs 19 (the same upstairs); h02 and h04 (the ground floor has only shop furniture); h06 (shoes in bed, about 628-652, 370). ROADMAP line 218 (notes, letters and photos tell stories), line 303 (story traces, sealed-up houses).
findings.why: What makes a home in This War of Mine or Project Zomboid feel real is not the furniture types but the traces of the people. Here there is nothing to read. A Thai player notices the missing universal cues right away: a pile of slippers at the door (and nobody sleeps in shoes), clothes on a rail, a calendar from a gold shop or a temple, the high Buddha shelf, a mosquito net. Repetition across houses also makes going into a new house feel like a chore instead of a small discovery, which weakens the scavenging half of the core loop.
findings.suggestion: Add a household-story layer. Each house draws one household from a data table: old couple, family with small kids, students renting upstairs, shop owner living alone, someone who barricaded in and died, family who packed and fled. That choice sets (a) small props and floor decals baked into the ground chunk: slipper pile at the door, clothes rail or laundry, wall calendar, family photo, school uniform on a hanger, prayer mat, baby cot, mosquito net, medicine boxes, toys, a half-packed suitcase by the door, scattered clothes, boards on the INSIDE of the windows plus a corpse upstairs; (b) small loot biases (kids: milk powder; old couple: medicine; students: instant noodles and a laptop to take apart); (c) later, the Phase 4 note on the fridge. When sleeping, draw the feet bare (visual only).
findings.scope_check: Data tables plus small static props and decals drawn once into the chunk, so no per-frame cost. No character views; the barefoot sleeper is a TopRig drawing detail. If the story is picked from the house seed at load time, it may not need a GEN bump.

findings.title: Wrong objects for a home: shop drinks cooler as the fridge, toilets in the open, flats without doors
findings.observation: FACT: a glass-door drinks cooler with coloured bottles (a shop fridge) stands in every back kitchen (h03 about 480,410; 17; 09) and in every one of the 9 visible rooms of the nurses' flats (h09). The squat toilet sits open next to the stove (h03 about 715,305) and, in the flats, next to the bed in every room with no bathroom wall (h09 about 275,190 and 235,510 and the other rooms). Flat rooms open onto the corridor through gaps with no doors, no numbers and nothing outside them (h09, h10 openings about 285-350 and 670-735 at y 200-260). All flat rooms have the same contents in mirrored positions.
findings.evidence: h03, 17, 09 (the cooler); h09 and h10 (flats); h03 (open toilet). ROADMAP line 344 (condos split into separate homes, several families per building).
findings.why: Everyone in Thailand has lived with these. A home fridge is a solid 1- or 2-door fridge with magnets, often in the front room. A bathroom is its own small room with a door, a water basin and a dipper. A flat corridor is a row of numbered steel or wood doors with a pile of shoes outside each one. Open toilets beside beds and door-less cubicles make the flats read as a stable or a prison. Doors also matter for the online plan, where a condo becomes several claimable homes (ROADMAP line 344).
findings.suggestion: (1) A 'home fridge' furniture variant: solid door, magnets, a calendar stuck on it. Keep the glass cooler for shops only. (2) Bathroom as a 1x2-cell room with its own door and a water basin, in the shophouse prefabs and in each flat unit. (3) Flats: a real door on every unit (the door system exists), a number plate, a shoe-pile decal outside each door, a laundry rail at the window, and a different household per unit from L1.
findings.scope_check: Fridge = one small art variant. Bathrooms and flat doors are prefab and big_plans data edits, so a GEN bump; batch them. No views, and the props are static.

findings.title: The main roads are nearly empty, but a city that tried to flee would be gridlocked
findings.observation: FACT: the arterial roads in view hold only a few vehicles. v01 (Ratchawithi): one parked car in view. v05 (Phahon Yothin at night): two wrecks plus kerb parking. 12_ratchawithi: six lanes with three wrecks. 02_phahon_bts: two wrecks under the BTS. ROADMAP line 197 already plans searching car trunks, sounding horns and siphoning fuel; line 314 makes every city vehicle climbable; zombies already bang cars and set off alarms.
findings.evidence: v01, v05, 12_ratchawithi, 02_phahon_bts; ROADMAP lines 197, 314, 393 (escape by vehicle, roof or canal).
findings.why: The real picture of an evacuating Bangkok is outbound lanes locked solid: doors open, suitcases on roofs, motorbikes threading between the cars. Empty roads make the city look cleared, not fled from. A jam also creates the vehicle choice you are missing. Cars can't get through, so a bike is precious. Car roofs become an escape path above the zombies. Trunks become loot. A zombie bumping one car sets off an alarm chain, which is danger you caused. That feeds 'go out, danger, decide' directly.
findings.suggestion: In the zone file, mark 1-2 evacuation directions (for example Phahon Yothin northbound). city_gen fills only the outbound half of those roads with lines of box vehicles from V1: gaps of 0.3-1 cell, a 1-cell bike gap between lanes, some doors open, luggage on roofs, a few burnt out. The inbound half stays mostly clear. Add searchable trunks and gloveboxes as rows in the action table. Cap vehicles per chunk.
findings.scope_check: Uses the existing props plus V1 and V2; placement is data. Static, baked once, so no per-frame cost beyond the existing alarm and zombie code. GEN bump, batched with V2 and V4.

findings.title: The delivery box and basket are decoration; the bike can't carry loot home
findings.observation: FACT: an orange delivery box is drawn on the ridden bike (v01, v03, v05) and on parked bikes (v13 top-left, a green box in 02 about 330,140). vehicles.cfg lists speed, accel, fuel, use, noise, hp, offroad and electric (lines 8-16) and has no storage field. ROADMAP line 385: the game lacks 'something you want' and 'a reason to take the risk'.
findings.evidence: v01, v03, v05, v13, 02_phahon_bts; data/vehicles.cfg lines 8-16; ROADMAP line 292 (the core loop) and line 385.
findings.why: In Bangkok the bike's everyday job is carrying things: a delivery box, a front basket of groceries, a gas bottle between the feet. In a scavenging loop, 'take the bike and bring home 6 more items' is a real decision (noise and fuel against more loot). It makes the bike worth protecting, and a delivery box becomes a coveted find.
findings.suggestion: Add a `store` column to vehicles.cfg (under-seat, 1-2 slots per model). Add fittable parts as items: front basket for wave, cub and scoopy (+2), delivery box (+4, already drawn), rack straps (one big item such as an LPG bottle or jerrycan). Open storage with E like furniture. A loaded bike picks up speed more slowly, e.g. accel x (1 - load / (2 x capacity)).
findings.scope_check: Data plus the existing storage and inventory UI. The box art already exists; the basket is one small piece of bike art in the existing 4 bike views. No character views, no per-frame cost.

findings.title: The bike should sleep inside the shophouse behind the shutter, like every Thai family's does
findings.observation: FACT: every bike in the screenshots is parked outside (h01, art_01, 18 bottom, v20). No interior contains a bike (h02, h04, 17, 18). From the brief: getting a bike running is an 8 s hotwire or a KEY_CHANCE dice roll. ROADMAP line 126 includes vehicles in ownership; lines 340-341 cover home claiming and lockable cupboards.
findings.why: It's the daily Bangkok ritual: at night the scooter is rolled into the shop and the rolling shutter comes down. It is the most natural link between 'vehicles' and 'living'. 'Going home' becomes riding in and pulling the shutter down, and the bike inside a closed house is safe. A key found in the house (a drawer by the altar, a hook by the door) turns the key from a dice roll into a search, which feeds scavenging.
findings.suggestion: Let the player ride or push a bike through an open rolling-shutter shop front into the ground-floor room and park it against a side wall, never in the doorway (this keeps your 'bikes never in shop fronts or doors' rule). Inside with the shutter down = not visible to zombies or other players. A share of homes spawn with the family's scooter inside and its key in that house's furniture loot (ties into L1's households). When ownership arrives, the bike belongs to the home.
findings.scope_check: Existing bike views, rolling-shutter doors and furniture loot; no new views. Bikes spawning inside is a placement change, so a GEN bump (batch it). No per-frame cost. Check that shutter width and collision allow a bike through.

findings.title: Which new vehicles, and in what order, within the scope rules
findings.observation: FACT: only motorbikes can be ridden. ROADMAP line 229 plans the tuk-tuk and the long-tail boat. The scope rules forbid new character views and camera changes (ROADMAP lines 96-109). The user is asking about bicycles, skateboards, cars and military vehicles. vehicles.cfg: the quietest engine is the electric scooter at noise 60 (line 103), the loudest the sport bike at 420 (line 124).
findings.evidence: ROADMAP lines 96-109, 229, 386 (few systems, many collisions); data/vehicles.cfg lines 98-107 and 119-127.
findings.why: OPINION: each new vehicle should be a different trade-off in systems you already have (noise, fuel, carrying, safety from bites, getting through jams), not just a different look. A car is actually CHEAPER in character art than a bike: the driver is inside, so only a head shows through the windscreen and no clothing template needs a new view.
findings.suggestion: Order: (1) Bicycle: noise about 30, no fuel, speed about 105-115 (just above the 95 sprint), stamina drain; the pedalling pose uses the existing rider anchors; a thin frame drawn in the existing bike views; a Thai 'housewife bike' with a front basket (V6). It creates a stealth versus speed choice. (2) Tuk-tuk (already in the ROADMAP): the driver sits upright (existing seated rider pose, 4 views), 2 passengers reuse the pillion system, loud, carries a lot; body from the V1 box drawer. (3) Cars, pickup and van through the V1 drawer: can face any angle, driver hidden; safe from bites and a big trunk, but loud, thirsty, and blocked by V5 jams and narrow sois. (4) Army truck: rare and drivable, with its canvas back as storage; armoured vehicles only as static loot sites. Skateboard: skip (Bangkok's broken pavements, no role in the core loop), or a joke clothing-style item at most.
findings.scope_check: Bicycle and tuk-tuk: new poses in the existing 4 views, rig-driven, so clothes follow. Cars: box drawer plus a head in the window, no character views. Per-frame: one moving vehicle per player drawing polygons is cheap compared with characters, but measure after the first car.

findings.title: Ground-floor walls read as dark trenches, and some doors look free-standing
findings.observation: FACT: in the shophouse ground floor, walls are flat dark-grey whole cells. The kitchen/shop partition in h03 (about 440-760, y 490-560) and the side walls in h04 read like dark gaps or corridors. Upstairs walls (h05, 19) and hospital walls (20, 21) have a lighter rim and read better as walls. In h03 the inner door (crop c_h03_door, about 640-700, 125-265) and in art_01 the door at about (718,580) stand upright on the floor with no visible wall on either side. In a 4-cell-wide house, the 1-cell walls take a large share of the width.
findings.why: OPINION: RimWorld and Prison Architect also use 1-tile walls, and they read as solid because the wall top is light, there is a short visible face and a contact shadow. Here, flat dark cells read as holes, so rooms look like cells cut out of darkness instead of plastered rooms. Doors that stand alone make the partitions unclear: is the toilet a room or not?
findings.suggestion: Keep whole-cell walls (engine) but change how they are drawn in the ground chunk: a light plaster or painted-brick top with a highlight, a 2-3 px darker south face (3/4) where the wall meets floor to its south, and a thin contact shadow on the floor. Draw doors inside the wall cell with a frame (jambs in the wall colour) so they read as 'a door in a wall'. Use the same rim style on every storey.
findings.scope_check: Drawing only, baked into static chunks: no per-frame cost, no GEN bump, no views.

findings.title: From upstairs, a flat lavender slab hides the soi right outside your front door
findings.observation: FACT: in h07 (upstairs front room of the gold shop), a flat lavender slab about 2 cells deep (about 415-800, 455-575), with a lighter top edge and one pole at about (447,600), covers the soi in front of the house. It has no sign, awning stripes or detail (crop c_h07_slab). Whether it is meant as the lower facade or the canopy (กันสาด), it reads as a market tarp and hides exactly the cells in front of the door. Only the parked bikes further south (y about 640) stay visible.
findings.evidence: h07 (compare v02 or h01, where the same shop front has a red sign and a striped awning).
findings.why: In real life the upstairs front window is where you watch the soi: who is at the door, is anyone coming. For a survival home it is the key lookout. Hiding those 2 cells under a blank slab removes that moment and makes the house feel like a box sitting on top of a tarp.
findings.suggestion: When the player is on storey 2 or higher, draw the lower facade or canopy as a real concrete canopy (กันสาด) at most 1 cell deep, with an edge line and a stain, at reduced alpha. Or draw characters under it as silhouettes on top. Make the upstairs front windows 'look out' spots (the SEATS system could let you sit by the window and watch).
findings.scope_check: Drawing and layer order only, no views, no GEN bump. It is part of the building drawing, so not a per-frame redraw of characters.

findings.title: Furniture hugs the walls; room centres are empty floor
findings.observation: FACT: in the hospital ground floor (20), the rooms have furniture only along the walls, and roughly 60-70% of each room is bare floor. In the hospital wards (21), beds line the walls with empty middles. In the shophouse, the middle room upstairs holds only the roof hatch (h05, 19), and the middle room downstairs holds boxes, the altar and the safe, all against walls (h04). There is no eating table, TV corner or floor mattress anywhere.
findings.evidence: 20_hospital_ground, 21_hospital_floor3, h04, h05, 19.
findings.why: Thai homes are dense and centred. The middle of a shophouse ground floor is where the family eats (low table or folding table with plastic stools), watches TV, parks the bike (V7) and where the kid does homework. Empty centres read as a showroom or an empty rental. Centre furniture also gives cover and line-of-sight breaks in fights, and more places to sit (SEATS).
findings.suggestion: Add a 'centre piece' slot per room type in the prefab and big_plans furniture tables: eating (folding table plus plastic stools, or a low table with a mat), TV (sofa, TV cabinet, fan), sleeping (mattress on the floor with a mosquito net), work (sewing machine, a desk with a school bag), waiting room (rows of steel chairs). Choose from the L1 household.
findings.scope_check: Data rows plus a few new static furniture drawings. Prefab edits mean a GEN bump (batch with L2). No views, no per-frame cost.

findings.title: Roofs are big empty slabs with no parapet; Bangkok rooftops are cluttered living space
findings.observation: FACT: in h08, each shophouse roof is a flat grey or terracotta slab about 4-5 x 13 cells with a hatch, 1-3 AC units, a blue barrel and nothing along its edge. A line of small coloured squares crosses roofs in h08 (y about 258 and 312) and 18 (y about 215). It is ambiguous whether this is bunting or laundry.
findings.evidence: h08_on_roof_z3, 18_shop_inside_wide, 17 (top-left line). The brief: the rooftop water tank and rain filling already exist as systems.
findings.why: The roof is where the player escapes, collects rain water and looks out, so it is part of 'home'. Real Bangkok shophouse roofs have laundry lines with shirts, towels and sarongs, water tanks on steel stands, potted chillies and basil, a satellite dish, rebar stubs sticking up from the columns for a future floor, a corrugated lean-to, and low parapets between neighbours. Empty slabs read as unfinished game art.
findings.suggestion: Add a roof-dressing data table per household (L1): laundry line with real garment shapes sagging between two poles, a water tank on a stand (the tank system already exists, so show it), pots, a dish, rebar stubs, a lean-to. Draw a 1-2 px parapet line along each roof edge, with a gap where neighbouring roofs join so the 'hop to the next roof' route is readable.
findings.scope_check: Static props and edge lines baked into chunks: no per-frame cost, no views. Rooftop props placed from the house seed at load time might avoid a GEN bump.

verdicts.fact_check: Confirmed in code. street_prop.gd:263-276 (_car_end) and 335-357 (_thai_end) draw north-south vehicles as a top-down rectangle 14 units wide plus a 5-unit dark front strip. Side-on vehicles (_car_side 235-260, _thai_side 281-330) show a full-height side and no roof top. Every end-on vehicle uses the headlight end (street_prop.gd:271-272, 354-355), and there is no rear drawing. Wrecks rotate the whole side or end drawing about its middle (street_prop.gd:447), which gives the 'ramp' look. Screenshots agree: v11 and v16 look like flat stickers with the player overlapping them, while the side-on bus in v17 reads well. One correction: 'bake each prop into a texture' is not needed. StreetProp already draws once through MeshCanvas in _draw (street_prop.gd:136-139), and Godot caches it until queue_redraw.
verdicts.reason: The problem is real and one of the main reasons vehicles feel off. But a general 3D box projector is a bigger step than this needs, and it could lose the hand-shaped charm of the side views (the bus). The BODY table (street_prop.gd:15) already holds per-kind heights and lengths, so a data-driven end view is half built.
verdicts.revised_observation: Vehicles parked north-south are drawn from almost straight above (the top of the car plus a 5-unit bumper strip), so they have no height in a world where buildings show a full front wall. Side-on vehicles show a full side but no roof. So the same car looks like two different objects depending on how it is parked, and end-on vehicles only ever show their front.
verdicts.revised_suggestion: Step 1 (S-M): rewrite _car_end and _thai_end so the end facing south is drawn at full height, in the same projection as buildings. That means bumper, lights, plate, windscreen or rear window up to the roof line, with the roof, bonnet or bed length drawn above it. Take the heights from BODY and extend BODY to car, taxi, tuktuk and army. Add a rear-end variant (tail lights, and for the songthaew the open back with benches and a step), picked by the facing rule in V4. Step 2 (S): give side views a thin roof strip on top. For wrecks, limit the tilt of side views, or use end views for the tilted ones. Step 3 (later, when cars become drivable): generalise into the box drawer the analyst describes.

verdicts.fact_check: Mostly correct, with one overstatement. Units: a bike is about 30 units long, i.e. 1.9 m (bike_art.gd:4, wheels at -10 and +11 with radius 4.4), and a person is about 29 units tall, so 1 unit is about 6 cm. With VEHICLE_SCALE 1.6 (street_prop.gd:10, applied in world.gd:241-242): sedan side view 31 units becomes 50, about 3.1 m (real 4.5). Van 34 units becomes 54, about 3.4 m (real 4.7-5.3). Bus 92 becomes 147, about 9.3 m. Tuk-tuk 16 becomes 26, about 1.6 m, which is SHORTER than a parked scooter (v13: the white scooter looks bigger than the tuk-tuk). Army truck (street_prop.gd:681-695) is 12 units tall, 19 after scaling, about 1.2 m against a person at about 1.8 m (v18: the roof sits at the player's shoulder). However, the sedan's HEIGHT is fine: roof 17 units, 27 after scaling, about 1.7 m. The problem is length (60-70% of real), the tuk-tuk (about 50%) and the army truck's height (about 40%), not everything being 55-70%. 'Needs a GEN bump' is overstated: _size_vehicles (city_gen.gd:1262-1287) is a post-pass that draws no random numbers, written exactly so that vehicle footprints can change without resetting cities (an overhang is accepted).
verdicts.reason: Right diagnosis. The rule 'squeeze distances, not the things a body touches' matches the prefab README (a cell is about a metre, shophouses at real size). Vehicles are the one exception. But the fix should target the worst offenders first, and it can skip the GEN bump.
verdicts.revised_observation: Parked vehicles are the only objects not at real size. Car, van, pickup and songthaew LENGTHS are 60-70% of real. A tuk-tuk is shorter than a scooter parked next to it. The army truck is about 40% of its real height, so it is shorter than the survivor. Car heights are about right.
verdicts.revised_suggestion: Replace the global VEHICLE_SCALE with a per-kind scale or per-kind BODY sizes. Priority order: army truck (height about 2.5x, length about 1.5x), tuk-tuk (length about 2x; fix together with V4's 3-wheel silhouette), then car, taxi, van, pickup and songthaew (length about 1.4x, keep height), then the bus (about 1.2x). Update roof_spot, roof_area, middle and draw_shift (street_prop.gd:21-99), which all read VEHICLE_SCALE, and add the extra cells in the _size_vehicles post-pass. That avoids a GEN bump, at the cost of occasional small overhangs. Changing VEHICLE_CELLS itself (city_gen.gd:38) does shift the RNG and needs the GEN bump, so leave that for the batched bump.

verdicts.fact_check: The look is confirmed in v01 (hunched, fists near the face) and v03 (hands at head height, elbows winged). But the suggestion to 'make anchors per bike class as data' ALREADY EXISTS: BIKE_SEATS in bike_art.gd:40-53 gives seat, bars and pegs per model. The real cause is mechanical. The bars sit about 15 units ahead of the seat (click: seat -7, bars +8), but ARM is only 8.6 (rig.gd:222-225). So Rig._anchored (rig.gd:351-372) leans to its 0.3 rad cap and then slides the hips forward up to 5 units: the most hunched posture it allows. In front and back views the depth shift (bike_art.gd:110-113, DEPTH 0.35) lifts the bars about 5 units, so the hands end up above the shoulders (shoulders at hips+8.6). Elbows prefer to point sideways (rig.gd:379) and knees point outward (rig.gd:386). The mirror-stalk point is a nitpick: _bars (bike_art.gd:293-297) draws stalks in the front and back views, and the rider's hands cover them.
verdicts.reason: High visibility (on screen every second of riding) and cheap, but it has to be fixed in the rig and the anchor numbers, not by adding a new data layer.
verdicts.revised_observation: Riders on 110-160 cc scooters sit hunched like sport riders, and from behind their hands are at head height with elbows and knees splayed. The per-model anchor table exists. The bars are simply further away than the rig's arms can reach, so the rig's fallback is maximum lean plus sliding forward. In end views, the depth shift pushes the bars above shoulder height.
verdicts.revised_suggestion: (1) In Rig._anchored, slide the hips forward first and lean only for the rest, and cap lean per model: about 0.05 for step-through and scooters, 0.3 for sport. Or pull scooter bars.x in by 3-4 units in BIKE_SEATS and nudge the drawn bars to match. (2) In front and back views, clamp each hand to about 1-2 units below shoulder height, and use an elbow preference of (±0.4, 1), i.e. down and slightly out. (3) For models not in ASTRIDE (step-throughs), set the knee preference inward so the knees stay inside the legshield. Check against v01, v02 and v03 crops.

verdicts.fact_check: Confirmed. Tuk-tuk (street_prop.gd:372-384): a flat rectangle with 2 equal wheels and a fringe, which reads as a food cart (v13). Songthaew and pickup end views are the same red rectangle (street_prop.gd:347-349). The bus route box is a plain orange bar (street_prop.gd:299-300). Facing: every end-on vehicle shows headlights at the south end. The analyst missed that every SIDE-ON vehicle faces east too (headlight at x=30 in _car_side, x=L in _thai_side, and world.gd:242 only applies a positive scale, never a flip). Parked traffic sits in lanes [0, 1, wd-2, wd-1] on both sides (city_gen.gd:921). So about half of all parked vehicles, on both axes, face against left-hand traffic: e.g. v18 red car in the west half facing south, v16 songthaew likewise. 'Parking rule = GEN bump' is wrong. Facing can be worked out at load or draw time from which half of the road the prop sits in, with no random numbers and no change to placement.
verdicts.reason: Strong realism point for Thai players, and cheap. The facing rule needs no GEN bump, and the rear view it needs doubles as the fix for the songthaew's identity.
verdicts.revised_observation: The tuk-tuk reads as a food cart. The songthaew, pickup and van are the same box end-on. Every parked vehicle faces south or east whatever lane it is in, so about half face against Thailand's left-hand traffic.
verdicts.revised_suggestion: (1) Facing, S, no GEN bump: in World when the StreetProp is made (world.gd:237-242), look up the road rect containing the prop. For east-west roads, flip scale.x for props in the south half, so the north half faces east and the south half faces west. For north-south roads, the west half shows the REAR end (tail lights) and the east half the front. Wrecks stay random. (2) Silhouettes, S-M, as BODY rows: tuk-tuk with 1 front wheel and 2 rear, a narrow cab nose and a curved canopy; songthaew rear with two benches, a step and a grab rail; pickup bed with side walls and cargo; van with a high roof and a route card; bus route number in the box; white or yellow plates as a 2-colour rectangle. Do it together with V1 step 1.

verdicts.fact_check: The core claim is stronger than stated. 11 of the 12 shophouse prefabs (all except the minimart 'store') share IDENTICAL first 6 rows (WWBWWW / WT.WJW / WG.dqW / WK.WWW / Wf..FW / WWdWWW), and all but the clinic share an identical 'floor 2:' block (checked by diffing data/prefabs/*.txt). Some specifics are wrong. Every upstairs front room already has a Buddha shelf 'I' (hiphra; the 'gold-trimmed cabinet' in h07 is that shelf). home.txt already places shoes at the door 'j', TV 'v', sofa 'O', Buddha shelf 'I' and a bike 'e' inside. The 'table and stools' decor 'r' exists but no shophouse prefab uses it. The shoes on the sleeper are confirmed in h06 (about 620-660, 370).
verdicts.reason: This is the biggest reason homes feel like a chore. The fix can mostly avoid a GEN bump by using the codebase's own pattern: _shop_fronts (city_gen.gd:1183-1202) adds decor last, from each building's own seed, 'so the rest of the city and the saves come out exactly as before'.
verdicts.revised_observation: Every shophouse, whatever its trade, has the same back kitchen and the same upstairs, object for object. Household cues exist as decor types (shoes, TV, sofa, Buddha shelf, table and stools), but only the plain 'home' prefab uses some of them. No house tells you who lived there or how they left.
verdicts.revised_suggestion: (1) No GEN bump: add a household pass after _shop_fronts that picks a household from rec.seed with its own RNG (old couple, family with kids, students renting upstairs, owner alone, fled in a hurry, barricaded and died). It appends only NON-blocking decor to free FLOOR cells: shoe pile, clothes rail, calendar, photo, uniform, mosquito net, toys, a half-packed suitcase, scattered clothes, the 'r' table and stools in the middle room where a 1-cell path stays clear. It also biases loot at search time (milk powder, medicine, noodles). (2) Batched GEN bump later: write 3-4 alternative back halves and upstairs layouts (bathroom on the other side, kitchen open to the back yard, three small bedrooms, a rented floor of mattresses) so layouts vary too. (3) Draw the sleeper barefoot (TopRig, visual only).

verdicts.fact_check: Fridge: confirmed. furniture_prop.gd:139-145 draws every 'fridge' as a glass-door cooler with coloured bottles and a blue base, whatever data.table is (home kitchens use table 'home'). Shophouse toilet: WRONG. The prefab rows 'WT.WJW' / 'WG.dqW' / 'WK.WWW' make a closed 1x2 bathroom (jar J above toilet q) with walls and an inner door 'd'. It only LOOKS open in h03 because the open side door is drawn face-on like a free-standing panel and the walls read as dark gaps (see L3). Flats: confirmed, but the root cause is systemic. big_plans.gd:231-242 puts the tap and toilet right beside the bed with no partition. Upper-floor doorways are open because _build_storey turns 'd' into FLOOR (city_gen.gd:438, 450-453). Doors only exist on storey 0 (city_gen.gd:505-508), so 'the door system exists' does not apply up there.
verdicts.reason: The fridge and the flats are right. The shophouse bathroom claim is wrong. Flat doors are not a data edit: they need doors on storeys, which also matters for sleeping upstairs and for ROADMAP 344 (condos split into homes).
verdicts.revised_observation: Every fridge, including in home kitchens and flat units, is drawn as a shop drinks cooler. Flat units have the toilet in the open beside the bed, and no door. That is because no door exists on any storey above the ground (doorways up there are left as open floor). The shophouse bathroom is already its own small room with a door. It just doesn't read as one.
verdicts.revised_suggestion: (1) S, no GEN bump: in furniture_prop.gd, branch on data.table == 'home' and draw a solid 1- or 2-door fridge with magnets and a calendar; keep the cooler for shop tables. (2) Flat bathroom: in big_plans 'unit', wall off a 1x2 corner with a doorway (a GEN bump; batch it). (3) Doors on storeys (see missed item M3), then a number plate and a shoe-pile decal outside each flat door.

verdicts.fact_check: Partly right. Parked traffic is length/7 per road on the outer lanes, with a 1-cell gap rule (city_gen.gd:917-923). Wrecks are length/22 per road, and pile-ups of 2-4 wrecks sit at 65% of junctions (city_gen.gd:997-1018). So the roads are dotted with cars, not jammed. Searching trunks, sounding horns and siphoning fuel are planned (ROADMAP:197). 'GEN bump' is avoidable: a last pass with its own RNG that only appends street_props keeps earlier prop ids stable (world.gd:233 uses the index as the id for cars you stand on) and leaves the rest of the city unchanged.
verdicts.reason: A good realism and gameplay direction (bikes thread through, car roofs as escape routes). But a jam with nothing to search is just scenery, and the planned trunk search should come first. Jams also cut through the main road network, which is the bike's main route, so keep bike gaps.
verdicts.revised_observation: Arterials show scattered parked cars and pile-ups at junctions, but nothing that reads as a city that tried to flee. Parked cars can't be searched yet (planned).
verdicts.revised_suggestion: First make existing car, taxi, van and pickup props searchable (trunk and glovebox as Interact actions with a loot table), as ROADMAP phase 2 plans. Then add an 'evacuation' pass run last, with its own seed. On 1-2 outbound road halves marked in the zone file, place lines of vehicles (sized per V2) with 1-cell bike gaps between lanes, luggage on some roofs, some doors open and a few burnt, and cap them per chunk. Keep ids stable by appending.

verdicts.fact_check: Confirmed: vehicles.cfg has no storage field, and a vehicle record (vehicles.gd:9, 68-70) has no container. The box and basket are already chosen per bike from its seed (BikeArt.extra_of, bike_art.gd:99-100; box on wave, click and pcx; basket on wave and scoopy). But 'S' is underestimated. Containers are furniture records tied to a fixed cell and storey (city_gen.gd:460). A container that moves with the bike, is saved in the vehicle delta (vehicles.gd:370-377) and is opened through the inventory UI is new plumbing.

But while food and water are plentiful (ROADMAP:385: food for 5 days, water for 3, loot in every house), extra carrying space matters less until scarcity arrives. It also needs keys and ownership first (missed item M2), otherwise anyone can ride off with your loaded bike.

missed.title: Riding at speed you see less than a second ahead
missed.observation: The camera zooms out only on roofs and at death (main.gd:1196-1200). While riding it only leads 0.3 s of travel, capped at 48 px (main.gd:106-108, 1029-1037). At the default zoom 4 on a 1280x720 window the view is 320x180 world px, so riding north or south you see about 90 + 48 = 138 px (about 8.6 cells) ahead. At 145-182 px/s (most models; the sport bike 250) that is about 0.55-0.95 s of warning. In v02 the rider is at y about 300 of 720, with about 6.5 cells of soi visible ahead. East-west is better (about 13 cells).
missed.why: Riding feels twitchy and blind. You hit wrecks and zombies you had no chance to see, especially in sois where roofs already hide cells (the known issue). Real riders read the road 3-5 s ahead. This is a big part of why riding 'feels off' even though the bike art is good.
missed.suggestion: Speed-based zoom-out, reusing the roof_k pattern at main.gd:1199: want = play_zoom * lerp(1.0, 0.72, clamp(ride_speed / 180, 0, 1)), easing back over about 1 s after slowing. Raise CAM_LEAD_MAX to about 90 px and weight the lead more on the vertical axis, since the screen is shorter that way. Optionally stretch the headlight cone with speed.
missed.scope_check: Not a new camera angle or rotation (auto-zoom already exists for roofs). Data and constants in main.gd. Per-frame: more visible area means more props and characters drawn, so measure with F3 or ?bench on the web build.

verdicts.direction_check: The direction is sound, but it needs re-scoping and some fact correction. (1) The two rules hold up against the code. 'Anything a body touches is life-size; only distances are squeezed' matches the prefab README (a cell is about a metre, shophouses at real size), and vehicles are the one exception (VEHICLE_SCALE 1.6: lengths 60-70%, the tuk-tuk shorter than a scooter, the army truck about 40% of its height; car heights are already right). 'Every solid shows its top plus its south face' is the correct cure for the end-on 'stickers'. (2) Don't bundle everything into one GEN bump. The codebase already has a no-reset pattern: post-passes that run last and use each building's own seed (_size_vehicles, _shop_fronts, _zone_exits). Vehicle facing from the road half, per-kind sizes via _size_vehicles, the household layer, home fridge art, wall and door drawing, key placement and storey doors can all avoid a reset. Keep a single later bump for real layout changes: prefab variants, flat bathrooms, and jams if they can't be appended. (3) Scope the 'box vehicle drawer'. First do end views at full height plus a rear variant using the existing BODY table; generalise when cars become drivable, which is an L project because of box collision. (4) Reorder by feel. First the always-on-screen riding fixes (rider posture via rig lean and slide and the end-view anchors; speed-based zoom and camera lead). Then vehicle end views, sizes and left-hand facing. Then prefab and household variety (11 of 12 prefabs share an identical back half and upstairs, the strongest 'every house is the same' cause). Then keys and ownership, then the bike inside the home, then storage, then new vehicles (bicycle, then tuk-tuk, then cars). (5) Several claims were wrong and should not reach the user as facts. The shophouse toilet is already an enclosed bathroom with a door (it only reads as open because of the wall and door drawing). Every upstairs already has a Buddha shelf. home.txt already has shoes, TV, sofa and a bike. Roof dressing already exists. Per-model rider anchors already exist. The sharper root causes are: identical prefab blocks, doors existing only on storey 0, one shop-cooler drawing for every fridge, a rig that hunches when the bars are out of reach, and a camera that doesn't widen with speed.
